newsitem.title: ITALY: Eridania sees brighter outlook for 1997.
newsitem.headline: Eridania sees brighter outlook for 1997.

text.p: Europe's largest agribusiness group, Eridania Begin-Say, expects lower raw material farm prices to continue to fuel a profits recovery into 1997, while industry overcapacity problems should ease this year.
Analysts forecast that the group's 1996 operating income will be down around seven to 10 percent, reflecting higher prices paid for the 1995 harvest.
But sources at Eridania said by the second half of last year there was an improving trend and this should continue in 1997.
Prospects have improved due to lower farm prices, industry overcapacity in key areas being absorbed and the fact that there is no great capacity increase in the pipeline, they said.
The French company, listed on the Paris bourse but 50.4 percent owned by Italian group Montedison, has reported that first-half 1996 net profit fell nearly 10 percent.
But it says full-year profits should be largely in line with 1995's 1.53 billion francs ($280 million) due to lower finance charges after a fall in French interest rates.

Grain harvests in 1996 across most of western Europe and North America recovered from poor 1995 levels, pushing farm prices lower and grain quantities up, both benefiting one of the world's largest processors of farm products.
Eridania holds leading positions in North American and European oilseeds and maize (corn) processing and in the European sugar industry.

The U.S. maize crop was 26 percent higher in 1996 and North American maize prices are returning to levels not seen since the middle of 1995. Sunflower and soybean crops also recovered, while in Europe the olive oil crop, halved by drought in 1995, returned to more normal levels last year.

Eridania's top positions in France and Italy place it as Europe's equal number one sugar processor with German Suedzucker. It is also Europe's top starch maker and third largest oilseeds crusher after U.S. groups Archer Daniels Midland and Cargill.

In North America, Eridania is number three in oilseeds and one of the major corn millers producing starch and sweeteners along with other large groups such as ADM, CPC International, Cargill and Tate & Lyle's Staley unit.

This latter area has been a major problem for all players in an industry producing industrial starch and High Fructose Corn Syrup (HFCS) sweeteners, used in consumer goods, soft drinks and the food industry.

The U.S. HFCS market grows in volume by around two to five percent a year and extra industry capacity in 1995/96 hurt a commodity-based business that is very susceptible to price movements. But Eridania says the outlook looks brighter with a decline in immediate new capacity coming onto the market.

It aims to counter fluctuating commodity prices by its geographic spread and product mix and also by working closely with its big food and drink industry customers to ensure pricing pressure are held to a minimum.
"Price rises can be coped with but it is very sudden price movements that cause problems," one Eridania source said.

At Montedison, chief executive Enrico Bondi has continued to stress that it has no intention of selling its stake. In fact, Eridania makes up nearly 70 percent of Montedison's total annual sales and accounts for all Montedison's agribusiness interests.

Montedison and its sister company Compart, formerly Ferruzzi Finanziaria, held on to Eridania in 1993 when both groups almost collapsed under a debt mountain. So Montedison says that it is unlikely to sell off Eridania now prospects are looking up. ($1=5.48 French Franc)
